kids.text: Types of Solutions
Solid in solid: alloys (brass, bronze, German silver)
Gas in liquid: O₂ in water (aquatic life), CO₂ in soda
Liquid in liquid: ethanol in water
Solute + Solvent = Solution
Concentration of Solutions
Mass % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100
Volume % = (volume of solute / volume of solution) × 100
ppm = (parts of component / total parts) × 10⁶
Mole fraction: xA = nA / (nA + nB); sum of all = 1
Molarity (M): moles of solute per litre of solution; temperature-dependent
Molality (m): moles of solute per kg of solvent; temperature-independent
Solubility
Like dissolves like: polar solutes in polar solvents
Saturated solution: in dynamic equilibrium (dissolution = crystallisation)
Solubility of Solids in Liquids
Increases with temperature if dissolution is endothermic (Le Chatelier)
Decreases with temperature if dissolution is exothermic
Pressure has no significant effect
Solubility of Gases in Liquids
Henry's Law: p = KH × x (partial pressure ∝ mole fraction)
KH is large → lower solubility at given pressure
Solubility decreases with rise in temperature (exothermic dissolution)
Applications: soda carbonation, scuba tanks (He + N₂ + O₂), decompression sickness (bends)
Vapour Pressure and Raoult's Law
Raoult's Law: partial pressure pA = xA × p°A (volatile components)
For non-volatile solute: p = xsolvent × p°solvent
Henry's law is a special case of Raoult's law (KH replaces p°)
Ideal Solutions
Obey Raoult's law over entire concentration range
ΔHmix = 0; ΔVmix = 0 (similar intermolecular forces)
Example: benzene–toluene, n-hexane–n-heptane
Non-ideal Solutions
Positive deviation: A-B weaker than A-A/B-B; vapour pressure > Raoult (e.g. ethanol-acetone)
Negative deviation: A-B stronger than A-A/B-B; vapour pressure < Raoult (e.g. chloroform-acetone)
Azeotropes
Binary mixture: same composition in liquid and vapour phase; constant boiling point
Minimum boiling azeotrope: large positive deviation (e.g. ethanol-water 95%)
Maximum boiling azeotrope: large negative deviation (e.g. HNO₃-water 68%)
Colligative Properties
Depend on number of solute particles, not their nature
Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure
(p° − p) / p° = xsolute = n₂/(n₁+n₂)
Used to find molar mass of solute
Elevation of Boiling Point
ΔTb = Kb × m (Kb = ebullioscopic/molal elevation constant)
M₂ = (Kb × w₂ × 1000) / (ΔTb × w₁)
Depression of Freezing Point
ΔTf = Kf × m (Kf = cryoscopic/molal depression constant)
Used in antifreeze solutions and for determining molar mass
Osmotic Pressure
π = CRT = (n₂/V)RT (R = gas constant)
Osmosis: flow of solvent from lower to higher concentration through semipermeable membrane
Isotonic: same osmotic pressure; hypertonic: higher; hypotonic: lower
Reverse osmosis: applied pressure > osmotic pressure (desalination)
Best method for large molar mass (polymers, proteins)
Abnormal Molar Masses
Van't Hoff factor i = observed / normal colligative property
i > 1: dissociation (e.g. NaCl, KCl in water)
i < 1: association (e.g. acetic acid dimerises in benzene)
Modified: ΔTb = i × Kb × m; ΔTf = i × Kf × m; π = iCRT
Electrochemical Cells
Galvanic (voltaic) cell: converts chemical energy → electrical energy (spontaneous)
Electrolytic cell: uses electrical energy → chemical energy (non-spontaneous)
Daniell cell: Zn|ZnSO₄||CuSO₄|Cu; EMF = 1.1 V
Galvanic Cells
Anode: oxidation (negative electrode); Cathode: reduction (positive electrode)
Salt bridge: maintains electrical neutrality; completes the circuit
Electrode potential: tendency of electrode to gain/lose electrons
Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE): reference electrode; E° = 0 V
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (SRP values from table)
Higher E° → stronger oxidising agent; lower E° → stronger reducing agent
ΔG° = −nFE°cell (relationship with Gibbs energy)
Nernst Equation
E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q
At equilibrium: E = 0; log Keq = nE°/0.0592
Used to calculate cell potential at non-standard conditions
Conductance of Electrolytic Solutions
Resistance R ∝ l/A; R = ρl/A
Conductance G = 1/R (unit: Siemens, S)
Conductivity κ = G × (l/A) = G × G* (cell constant)
Molar conductivity Λm = (κ × 1000) / M (M = molarity)
Variation with Concentration
Strong electrolytes: Λm = Λ°m − A√c (Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation)
Weak electrolytes: Λm increases sharply on dilution; degree of dissociation α = Λm/Λ°m
Kohlrausch's Law: Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋ (sum of ionic contributions)
Electrolysis
Faraday's 1st Law: mass deposited ∝ quantity of electricity (Q = It)
Faraday's 2nd Law: mass ∝ equivalent mass of substance
1 Faraday = 96500 C mol⁻¹ (charge of 1 mol electrons)
Electrolytic refining of copper: impure Cu → anode; pure Cu → cathode
Production of Na, Mg, Al by electrolysis of fused salts/oxides
Batteries
Primary Batteries (non-rechargeable)
Dry cell (Leclanche): Zn anode, MnO₂ cathode; 1.5 V
Mercury cell: Zn-Hg anode, HgO cathode; constant 1.35 V
Secondary Batteries (rechargeable)
Lead storage battery: Pb anode, PbO₂ cathode, H₂SO₄ electrolyte; 2V/cell
Nickel-cadmium cell: longer life; rechargeable
Fuel Cells: H₂-O₂ cell; converts chemical energy to electrical energy continuously (no recharging)
Corrosion
Electrochemical process: Fe acts as anode (oxidised), water/O₂ at cathode
Rust = Fe₂O₃·xH₂O
Prevention: painting, galvanising (Zn coating), alloying, cathodic protection
Rate of a Chemical Reaction
Rate = change in concentration / time: r = −d[R]/dt = +d[P]/dt
Average rate vs Instantaneous rate (tangent to concentration-time curve)
Units: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
Rate for 2A → B: r = −(1/2)d[A]/dt = +d[B]/dt
Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction
Concentration of reactants
Temperature
Catalyst
Surface area (for heterogeneous reactions)
Light (photochemical reactions)
Rate Law and Rate Constant
Rate = k[A]^m [B]^n (rate law / rate expression)
k = rate constant (specific reaction rate)
Order = m + n (sum of exponents in rate law; determined experimentally)
Molecularity: number of molecules in elementary step
Order can be zero, fractional, integer; molecularity always positive integer
Integrated Rate Equations
Zero Order
[R] = [R]₀ − kt
t½ = [R]₀/2k
k has units: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
First Order
ln[R] = ln[R]₀ − kt; or [R] = [R]₀e^(−kt)
t½ = 0.693/k (independent of initial concentration)
k has units: s⁻¹; e.g. radioactive decay, decomposition of H₂O₂
Temperature Dependence: Arrhenius Equation
k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) (A = pre-exponential/frequency factor; Ea = activation energy)
ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)[1/T₁ − 1/T₂]
Rate doubles for every 10°C rise (rule of thumb)
Activation energy: minimum energy needed for reaction to occur
Activated complex/transition state: unstable intermediate at energy maximum
Effect of Catalyst
Provides alternative pathway with lower activation energy
Does not change ΔH or equilibrium position; not consumed
Increases both forward and backward rate equally
Collision Theory
Reaction occurs when molecules collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation
Threshold energy = activation energy + average kinetic energy
Steric factor p: fraction of collisions with correct orientation
Rate = pZABe^(−Ea/RT) (Z = collision frequency)
The d-Block (Transition Elements)
Groups 3–12; partially filled d-orbitals in ground or ionic state
Four series: 3d (Sc–Zn), 4d (Y–Cd), 5d (La, Hf–Hg), 6d (incomplete)
General config: (n-1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²
Exceptions: Cr = [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Cu = [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (half/fully filled stability)
General Properties of Transition Elements
High melting and boiling points (strong metallic bonding via d-electrons)
High densities and hardness
Ionisation enthalpies: higher than s-block; irregular trends across series
Variable Oxidation States
Due to small energy difference between (n-1)d and ns electrons
Mn shows maximum OS (+7); most show +2 and higher
Magnetic properties: paramagnetic due to unpaired d-electrons
Catalytic properties: variable OS and ability to adsorb reactants on surface
Formation of coloured compounds/ions: d-d transition absorbs visible light
Tendency to form complex compounds with ligands
Alloy formation: similar atomic sizes, same crystal structure
Important Compounds of Transition Metals
Potassium Dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇)
Cr in +6 oxidation state; orange colour
Strong oxidising agent in acidic medium
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
Potassium Permanganate (KMnO₄)
Mn in +7 oxidation state; purple/violet colour
Powerful oxidising agent in acidic, neutral, alkaline media
Acidic: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺; Neutral: MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂; Alkaline: MnO₄⁻ → MnO₄²⁻
The Lanthanoids (f-Block, 4f Series)
Ce (58) to Lu (71); filling of 4f orbitals
Common OS: +3; some show +2, +4
Lanthanoid contraction: progressive decrease in ionic radii (poor shielding by 4f)
Consequence: 4d and 5d elements have almost same radii; similar chemistry
All paramagnetic; most are pale coloured; used in alloys, magnets, phosphors
The Actinoids (f-Block, 5f Series)
Th (90) to Lr (103); filling of 5f orbitals
Show wider range of OS than lanthanoids (5f, 6d, 7s close in energy)
Most are radioactive; U and Th are naturally occurring
Actinoid contraction similar to lanthanoid contraction
Werner's Theory
Primary valence: ionisable; satisfied by counter ions (oxidation state)
Secondary valence: non-ionisable; satisfied by ligands (coordination number)
Difference from double salts: complex ions retain identity in solution
Important Terms
Central metal atom/ion: Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor)
Ligand: Lewis base (electron pair donor); monodentate, bidentate, polydentate
Chelate: complex with polydentate ligand (more stable; chelate effect)
Coordination number: number of donor atoms directly bonded to metal
Coordination sphere: central atom + ligands in square brackets
Nomenclature
Cation named first, then anion
Ligands: anionic (-o), neutral (as is), cationic (-ium); listed alphabetically
Metal OS in Roman numerals in parentheses
Anionic complex: metal name + -ate suffix
Isomerism in Coordination Compounds
Stereoisomerism
Geometric (cis-trans): different arrangement of ligands; square planar and octahedral
Optical (mirror image, non-superimposable): d and l forms; shown by octahedral complexes
Structural Isomerism
Linkage isomerism: ambidentate ligand binds via different atoms (e.g. NO₂ vs ONO)
Coordination isomerism: interchange of ligands between cation and anion of complex
Ionisation isomerism: different anion in coordination sphere vs outside
Solvate isomerism: water inside vs outside coordination sphere
Bonding Theories
Valence Bond Theory (VBT)
Ligands donate electron pairs to empty hybrid orbitals of metal
Inner orbital complex (low spin): d²sp³, dsp²; outer orbital (high spin): sp³d²
Limitation: does not explain colour and magnetic properties quantitatively
Crystal Field Theory (CFT)
Ligands as point charges; d-orbitals split in crystal field
Octahedral: d-orbitals split into t₂g (lower) and eg (higher); Δo = crystal field splitting
Strong field ligands (CO, CN⁻): large Δo → low spin; weak field (F⁻, Cl⁻): small Δo → high spin
Colour: d-d transition; wavelength absorbed complementary to colour seen
Spectrochemical series: I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < py < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO
Metal Carbonyls
CO as ligand: σ-donor and π-acceptor (synergic bonding)
Ni(CO)₄: tetrahedral; Fe(CO)₅: trigonal bipyramidal; Cr(CO)₆: octahedral
Importance of Coordination Compounds
Haemoglobin: Fe²⁺ complex; oxygen transport in blood
Chlorophyll: Mg²⁺ complex; photosynthesis
Vitamin B₁₂: Co³⁺ complex
Cisplatin [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]: anticancer drug
EDTA: used in chelation therapy; water softening
Classification
Haloalkanes: halogen bonded to sp³ carbon (alkyl halides)
Haloarenes: halogen bonded to sp² carbon of aromatic ring
Types: primary, secondary, tertiary (based on C bearing X)
Allylic (C next to C=C), benzylic (PhCH₂X), vinylic, aryl halides
Nature of C–X Bond
C–X bond polar: C is δ+ due to higher electronegativity of X
Bond length increases: C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I
Bond strength decreases: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I
Preparation of Haloalkanes
From alcohols: ROH + HX → RX + H₂O (Lucas test); SOCl₂, PCl₃/PCl₅
Free radical halogenation of alkanes (Cl₂ or Br₂ in light)
Addition of HX to alkenes (Markovnikov rule)
Preparation of Haloarenes
Electrophilic substitution: X₂/FeBr₃ (benzene + Br₂)
Sandmeyer's reaction: ArN₂⁺ + CuX → ArX + N₂
Physical Properties
Boiling points: RI > RBr > RCl > RF; increase with chain length
Density: denser than corresponding alkanes (except RF)
Insoluble in water; soluble in organic solvents
Chemical Reactions of Haloalkanes
Nucleophilic Substitution (SN)
SN2: bimolecular; one step; inversion of configuration (Walden inversion); favoured by 1° RX
SN1: unimolecular; two steps; carbocation intermediate; racemisation; favoured by 3° RX
Nucleophiles: OH⁻, CN⁻, RO⁻, NH₃ replace X
Elimination (E2 / Dehydrohalogenation)
Conc. KOH/alcohol → alkene + HX (β-elimination)
Saytzeff rule: more substituted alkene is major product
Reaction with metals: Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na → R-R + 2NaX)
Grignard reagent: RX + Mg/dry ether → RMgX (extremely useful in synthesis)
Reactions of Haloarenes
Nucleophilic substitution difficult (C–X has partial double bond character)
Electrophilic substitution: X is o/p-directing and deactivating
Wurtz-Fittig: ArX + RX + 2Na → Ar-R
Fittig: 2ArX + 2Na → Ar-Ar (biaryl)
Polyhalogen Compounds
CHCl₃ (chloroform): anaesthetic; oxidises to COCl₂ (phosgene) in light/air
CCl₄: fire extinguisher; liver damage (toxic)
Freons (CFCs): refrigerants; deplete ozone layer
DDT: first chlorinated organic insecticide; persistent (non-biodegradable)
Classification
Monohydric: one –OH; dihydric: two –OH (glycol); trihydric: three –OH (glycerol)
Primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) based on carbon bearing –OH
Phenols: –OH directly on aromatic ring
Preparation of Alcohols
Hydration of alkenes: H₂O/H⁺ → Markovnikov addition
Reduction of carbonyl compounds: aldehydes → 1° alcohol; ketones → 2° alcohol (NaBH₄/LiAlH₄)
Grignard reagents: RMgX + carbonyl → alcohol after hydrolysis
Preparation of Phenols
From chlorobenzene: Dow process (high T, P, NaOH)
From cumene (isopropylbenzene): industrial method
From diazonium salts (Sandmeyer type)
Physical Properties
Boiling points: higher than alkanes/ethers due to H-bonding
Lower alcohols miscible with water; solubility decreases with chain length
Phenol slightly soluble in water; acidic (pKa ~10)
Chemical Reactions of Alcohols and Phenols
Reactions involving O–H bond cleavage
With Na: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂↑ (alkoxide)
Esterification: ROH + RCOOH ⇌ RCOOR + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄)
Reactions involving C–O bond cleavage
With HX: ROH + HX → RX + H₂O (Lucas test: ZnCl₂/HCl; 3°>2°>1°)
Dehydration with conc. H₂SO₄: at 443K → alkene; at 413K → ether
Oxidation
1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid (with K₂Cr₂O₇/KMnO₄)
2° alcohol → ketone
3° alcohol: not easily oxidised
Reactions of Phenol
Acidity: PhOH + NaOH → PhONa + H₂O (more acidic than alcohols)
Electrophilic aromatic substitution: OH is o/p-director (activating)
Kolbe's reaction: PhONa + CO₂/pressure → salicylic acid
Reimer-Tiemann: PhOH + CHCl₃/KOH → salicylaldehyde
Ethers
General formula: R–O–R'; simple (R=R') or mixed
Preparation: Williamson synthesis (RX + R'ONa → R–O–R' + NaX)
Physical: lower BP than alcohols (no H-bonding); slightly soluble in water
Chemical Reactions
C–O bond cleavage with HI or HBr (conc.): R–O–R' → RX + R'OH
Electrophilic substitution on aromatic ethers (o/p-director)
Aldehydes and Ketones
Structure and Nomenclature
Carbonyl group C=O; aldehydes have –CHO at chain end; ketones have C=O in middle
IUPAC: -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone); common: formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone
Preparation
Oxidation of 1° alcohols (aldehyde) and 2° alcohols (ketone)
Ozonolysis of alkenes
Aldehydes: Rosenmund reduction (RCOCl + H₂/Pd-BaSO₄); Stephen reduction
Ketones: Friedel-Crafts acylation (ArH + RCOCl/AlCl₃)
Physical Properties
Polar C=O; higher BP than alkanes; lower than alcohols (no H-bonding)
Lower members soluble in water (H-bonding with water)
Chemical Reactions
Nucleophilic addition: HCN, RMgX, NaHSO₃, H₂O (aldehydes more reactive than ketones)
Reduction: H₂/Ni or NaBH₄ → primary/secondary alcohol; Clemmensen → CH₂; Wolff-Kishner → CH₂
Oxidation: Tollens' test (Ag mirror); Fehling's test (Cu₂O brick red); only aldehydes
Aldol condensation: α-H present → β-hydroxy carbonyl compound → α,β-unsaturated (with base)
Cannizzaro reaction: no α-H → disproportionation (HCHO → HCOOH + CH₃OH)
Condensation with amines, hydroxylamine, semicarbazide → imine derivatives
Uses: HCHO as formalin (40%), bakelite; acetone as solvent; benzaldehyde in perfumery
Carboxylic Acids
Structure and Nomenclature
–COOH group; IUPAC: -oic acid; common: formic, acetic, propionic acids
Aromatic: benzoic acid (PhCOOH)
Preparation
Oxidation of primary alcohols, aldehydes, and alkylbenzenes
Hydrolysis of nitriles (RCN + H₂O/H⁺), esters, amides
Grignard reagent + CO₂ → RCOOH after hydrolysis
Physical Properties
High BP: H-bonding; dimers formed in vapour phase
Solubility in water decreases with chain length
Chemical Reactions
Acidity: RCOOH ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H⁺; electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity
Esterification: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H₂O (Fischer esterification)
Formation of acyl chloride (SOCl₂), anhydride, amide, ester
Reduction to 1° alcohol with LiAlH₄
Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH/CaO → RH + Na₂CO₃
Halogenation at α-position: Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction (Br₂/red P)
Classification and Nomenclature
Primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH), tertiary (R₃N) based on N-substitution
Aliphatic and aromatic amines; aniline = aminobenzene
IUPAC: alkan-1-amine; common: methylamine, dimethylamine, aniline
Preparation of Amines
Reduction of nitro compounds: RNO₂ + 6[H] → RNH₂ (Fe/HCl or H₂/Ni)
Ammonolysis of alkyl halides: RX + NH₃ → RNH₂ (then 2°, 3°, quaternary salt)
Reduction of nitriles: RCN + 4[H] → RCH₂NH₂ (LiAlH₄)
Reduction of amides: RCONH₂ + 4[H] → RCH₂NH₂ (LiAlH₄)
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: pure 1° amines; phenylamino phthalimide + RX + hydrolysis
Hofmann bromamide degradation: RCONH₂ + Br₂/NaOH → RNH₂ (loses 1 carbon)
Physical Properties
Lower amines: gases (fishy smell); higher: liquids/solids
Boiling points: 1°>2°>3° (H-bonding); lower than alcohols of similar mass
Solubility: lower amines soluble in water (H-bonding); decreases with MW
Chemical Reactions
Basic Character
Lone pair on N: acts as Lewis base (proton acceptor)
Basicity: aliphatic (2°>1°>3°>NH₃); aromatic amines less basic (lone pair delocalised)
Electron-donating groups increase basicity; electron-withdrawing decrease
Alkylation: R-NH₂ + RX → 2°, 3°, quaternary ammonium salt
Acylation: R-NH₂ + RCOCl → amide + HCl (conc. NaOH present)
Carbylamine reaction (1° amine only): RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + KOH → RNC (isocyanide, foul smell)
Reaction with HNO₂: 1° aliphatic → unstable diazonium salt (N₂ + alcohol)
Electrophilic aromatic substitution: NH₂ is strong o/p-director (activating)
Diazonium Salts
Preparation: ArNH₂ + NaNO₂ + HCl (0–5°C) → ArN₂⁺Cl⁻ (diazotisation)
Reactions Replacing N₂
Sandmeyer's reaction: CuX → ArX; CuCN → ArCN; CuOH → ArOH
Gattermann reaction: Cu powder + HX → ArX
ArN₂⁺ + H₃PO₂ + H₂O → ArH (reduction)
Coupling reaction: ArN₂⁺ + phenol/amine → azo dye (brilliant colours)
Importance: versatile intermediates for diverse aromatic compounds
Carbohydrates
General formula: Cx(H₂O)y; produced by photosynthesis
Classified by taste: sugars and non-sugars; by hydrolysis: mono, oligo, polysaccharides
Monosaccharides
Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆): aldohexose; open chain and cyclic (pyranose) forms
Glucose structure: open chain (6C, CHO at C1, OH at C2-C6); cyclic (α and β anomers)
Fructose: ketohexose (C2 ketone); sweeter than glucose
D and L sugars based on configuration at penultimate C
Disaccharides
Sucrose (cane sugar): glucose + fructose; non-reducing (no free –CHO/–OH)
Maltose (malt sugar): glucose + glucose; reducing sugar
Lactose (milk sugar): galactose + glucose; reducing sugar
Polysaccharides
Starch: storage in plants; amylose (helical) + amylopectin (branched)
Cellulose: structural in plants; β-1,4-glycosidic linkage; not digested by humans
Glycogen: storage in animals (liver, muscle); highly branched
Proteins
Polymers of α-amino acids; linked by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–)
20 essential amino acids; essential (not synthesised by body): must be taken in diet
Zwitter ion: amino acid with –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ at isoelectric point
Structure of Proteins
Primary: amino acid sequence (peptide bonds)
Secondary: α-helix or β-pleated sheet (H-bonds within/between chains)
Tertiary: 3D folding (disulfide bonds, H-bonds, van der Waals, hydrophobic)
Quaternary: multiple polypeptide subunits (e.g. haemoglobin = 4 subunits)
Fibrous proteins: insoluble, structural (e.g. keratin, collagen, myosin)
Globular proteins: soluble, functional (e.g. haemoglobin, enzymes, antibodies)
Denaturation: loss of native structure (not peptide bonds) by heat, acid, etc.
Enzymes
Biological catalysts; protein in nature (except ribozymes)
Highly specific (lock and key model; induced fit model)
Active site: specific region that binds substrate
Rate enhanced by 10⁶–10¹² times compared to uncatalysed
Affected by temperature, pH, inhibitors, cofactors
Vitamins
Organic compounds needed in small amounts; cannot be synthesised by body
Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K (stored in body; excess causes hypervitaminosis)
Water-soluble: B complex, C (not stored; deficiency causes disease quickly)
Deficiency diseases: A→night blindness; C→scurvy; D→rickets; B₁→beriberi; B₃→pellagra
Nucleic Acids
Polynucleotides; store and transfer genetic information
Nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate group
DNA: deoxyribose; double helix (Watson-Crick); A-T, G-C base pairing
RNA: ribose; single stranded; mRNA, tRNA, rRNA
DNA → RNA (transcription) → Protein (translation)
DNA fingerprinting: identifying individuals from DNA patterns
Hormones
Chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands into blood
Steroids (e.g. estrogen, testosterone): derived from cholesterol
Amino acid derivatives (e.g. adrenaline, thyroxine)
Polypeptides (e.g. insulin, oxytocin): regulate blood glucose, growth, etc.
